titre: “Primum Non Nocere” Is Not in the Hippocratic Oath
accroche: The formula attributed to the oath is not found there, and the closest Hippocratic text says something else
contenu_vulgarise:
“Primum non nocere,” first do no harm: it is commonly presented as the first rule of the Hippocratic oath. Yet it does not appear in the oath, and it is not read in this form in any text attributed to Hippocrates.

## What the Texts Say

In Francis Adams's English translation, the oath commits the physician to follow a regimen set for the benefit of his patients, to abstain from everything “deleterious and harmful,” to give no deadly drug even if asked for one, not to give an abortive pessary, and not to cut patients suffering from the stone. A general abstention clause does exist, then, but it sits within a series of specific prohibitions, and nothing places it before the patient's benefit. Neither the Latin formula nor its English equivalent, “first, do no harm,” appears in the text.

The closest sentence is found in another treatise of the corpus, *Epidemics* I. In the same translation, the physician must have in view, with regard to disease, “two special objects”: to do good, or to do no harm. Two details matter. First, the order: in this sentence, good comes first, and the abstention can be read as the fallback when good cannot be done. Second, the language: these texts are written in Greek, so the Latin formula is a later restatement.

## Where the Latin Comes From

Its origin remains debated. The historian Thomas Morris (2019) notes that a Greek-Latin dictionary by Bartholomeo Castellus rendered the passage of *Epidemics* in 1713 as “prodesse, aut non nocere”: to be useful, or to do no harm. He finds the Latin formula in the medical literature as early as 1814, in Alexis Boyer's *Traité des maladies chirurgicales* (*Treatise on Surgical Diseases*). Older work, including a 2005 article by Cedric Smith, had it born in 1860 with the English physician Thomas Inman, who attributed it to Thomas Sydenham; Morris does not find it in Sydenham's writings.

## The Shift

The inversion changes the meaning. “To do good or to do no harm” describes a trade-off: one seeks the benefit, and refrains when there is none. “First, do no harm” looks like a veto that would come before everything. As a first approximation, almost no medical act is harmless: an incision wounds, chemotherapy poisons, an injection hurts, and not acting can also harm. Read as an absolute rule, the formula would forbid medicine.

Between the trade-off of the Greek text and the veto of the Latin formula, medicine most often practices the former, as soon as benefit and risk lie in the same act.

repere.texte: In Francis Adams's English translation, Epidemics I asks the physician to aim at two objects, “to do good or to do no harm,” and the Hippocratic oath contains neither “primum non nocere” nor “first, do no harm.”
repere.source: Hippocrates, Of the Epidemics, Book I, trans. Francis Adams (MIT Internet Classics Archive)

carte.punch: “Primum non nocere” is not in the Hippocratic oath.
carte.idee: Neither the oath nor Epidemics I contains “primum non nocere.” The closest text asks to do good or to do no harm: a trade-off, not a veto. Thomas Morris finds it in the medical literature as early as 1814, in Alexis Boyer.

quiz.question: In the face of disease, what objectives does Epidemics I (Adams translation) set for the physician?
choix: To avoid above all any act capable of harm, whatever the expected benefit
To do good, or to do no harm
To recite the formula primum non nocere at the start of each treatment
To refrain from acting until the patient has given consent
quiz.explication: The passage places two objectives side by side: to do good, or to do no harm. It is not a veto that would come before any benefit, the Latin formula does not appear in it, and no consent from the patient is mentioned.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Hippocratic oath contain, in Adams's translation, about what the physician forbids himself?
choix: Specific prohibitions, such as the deadly drug or the pessary
The formula “first, do no harm” at the opening of the text
A single general principle, placed before any other rule
The obligation never to intervene surgically
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The oath lists specific prohibitions: no deadly drug, no abortive pessary, no cutting for the stone, with a clause of abstention from what is harmful among other commitments. It does not open with the formula “first, do no harm” and does not ban all surgery.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Castellus's dictionary (1713) show, according to Thomas Morris?
choix: That the formula primum non nocere dates from Hippocrates's time
That the oath was translated into Latin in the 18th century
That the passage of Epidemics was rendered in Latin as “prodesse, aut non nocere”
That Sydenham had already used the formula
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Castellus renders the passage of Epidemics as “prodesse, aut non nocere,” to be useful or to do no harm. This shows a Latin version close to the Greek sense, without proving that the formula primum non nocere existed in Hippocrates's time.
